summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition has been prohibited outright since the law signed in July 2023 banning gender-affirming surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents. A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the republic.

The republic sits within the North Caucasus, which the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. Trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the North Caucasus, Karachay-Cherkessia included, are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. Under the national extremist-designation regime the note records sentences of two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports year-on-year deterioration, covering the North Caucasus republics including Karachay-Cherkessia.

The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of material that makes minors interested in gender transition and applies to all age groups. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transition, and single-person foreign adoption is permitted only if that country recognises neither same-sex marriage nor gender transition.

Russian law provides no anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate-crime designation on those grounds. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent has stood at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex couples are ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, with neither marriage nor civil unions permitted.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 European LGBTI legal and policy ranking scores Russia at 2%, citing explicit bans and legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible.
tangentialFactors:
Military-related discussion in 2023 linked legal gender change to draft avoidance, with proposals aimed at preventing trans women from changing legal status from male to female without surgery; the Duma Speaker claimed about 2,700 such decisions had been made. President Putin stated on 30 September 2022 that teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable.

Enforcement of the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT public movement as extremist has included arrests of gay bar owners and fines or imprisonment for displaying the rainbow flag. Between March and May 2026, city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist, with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation.

Documented violence linked to sexual orientation in the wider North Caucasus includes the reported detention and torture of over 100 men in Chechnya since February 2017, with at least three extrajudicial killings reported on 1 April 2017, and a further purge reported in January 2019 with around 40 detained and two killed. An estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals were recorded across Russia between 2010 and 2020, with 365 fatalities.
localsOnly:
Residents of Karachay-Cherkessia diagnosed with gender dysphoria lose the right to adopt under the 2023 national statute, and the July 2020 constitutional amendment bars same-sex marriage. Russian law's removal of anti-discrimination and hate-crime protections applies equally to residents of the republic.

Systematic regional campaigns against LGBT people documented across the North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 affect residents directly, with Isteev's testimony indicating that private existence can expose local LGBTIQ+ people to violence, detention or forced return to their families.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the North Caucasus face treatment amounting to persecution rests on the UK Home Office's June 2025 assessment; whether Russian domestic courts or the Karachay-Cherkessia authorities apply comparable reasoning is not sourced here.

Isteev's account of year-on-year deterioration is a defender's testimony rather than a quantified series; no incident count specific to Karachay-Cherkessia is available in this inventory.

The 2023 extremist-designation sentences of two to six years, or six to ten for organising, are stated in the UK Home Office note without a citation to a specific Karachay-Cherkessia judgment; whether any such convictions have occurred within this republic is unresolved.
